\chapter{The People in the Sentence}
\label{ch:ml-aalukal}
\hlchaptermodality{71}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about somebody who is not in the room, at either level of respect, and I can say we in the two ways Malayalam requires.}

From cold: the five third-person and we-words, the front letter that points away, and the question each choice answers.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[avan / avaḷ]{\ml{അവൻ} / \ml{അവൾ} — the same front letter, on a person}

\label{lesson:ML-C71-avan-aval}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for \emph{this one} and the word for \emph{that one}. Say which front letter means near and which means far.

Now point at a person and say \emph{he}. \textbf{You have had the system since chapter forty-one and no word to use it on.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അവൻ} and \ml{അവൾ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{അവൻ}} — \emph{avan} — \textbf{he} \textbf{\ml{അവൾ}} — \emph{avaḷ} — \textbf{she}
\end{quote}

Both open with the same \textbf{\ml{അ}-} that makes \textbf{\ml{അത്}} mean \emph{that one}. The pointing system was never only about things; it has a column for people, and this is it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{a thing} & \textbf{a person} \\
\midrule
near & \ml{ഇത്} & — \\
far & \ml{അത്} & \ml{അവൻ} / \ml{അവൾ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The ending is what splits them}: \textbf{-\ml{ൻ}} for a man, \textbf{-\ml{ൾ}} for a woman. Those two endings turn up again on other words, and meeting them here is the cheapest place to learn them.

\begin{cousinweb}
These are the \textbf{familiar} words, the ones for somebody younger, a close friend, a child — the people you would address with \textbf{\ml{നീ}} rather than \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}}.

Tamil does the same thing with the same sounds, \emph{avaṉ} and \emph{avaḷ}, which is worth noticing because the two languages have been agreeing on the small grammatical words far more often than on the everyday nouns.

A step up in respect needs a different word, and it arrives in the next lesson.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ml{അവൻ}, \ml{അവൾ}
  \item which ending marks a woman
  \item the front letter all three of \ml{അവൻ}, \ml{അവൾ} and \ml{അത്} share
  \item which of \ml{നീ} and \ml{നിങ്ങൾ} these two words keep company with
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word is \emph{she}? (\textbf{\ml{അവൾ}}.) What does the \textbf{\ml{അ}-} at the front do? (Points away.) Are these the familiar words or the respectful ones? (Familiar.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[avar]{\ml{അവർ} — one word for \emph{they} and for a person you respect}

\label{lesson:ML-C71-avar}



\begin{quote}
Say the two words for \emph{you}, and say what makes the second one polite.

That same move is about to happen in the third person.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അവർ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{അവർ}} — \emph{avar} — \textbf{they}, and about one person, \textbf{he} or \textbf{she} respectfully
\end{quote}

The \textbf{-\ml{ർ}} on the end is a plural, and \textbf{Malayalam raises the register by making one person grammatically several} — the exact move that turned \textbf{\ml{നീ}} into \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}} back in chapter two.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{familiar} & \textbf{respectful} \\
\midrule
\ml{നീ} & \ml{നിങ്ങൾ} \\
\ml{അവൻ} / \ml{അവൾ} & \ml{അവർ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Learning it once buys it twice.} A habit met in the second chapter of the book turns out to be a rule of the language rather than a fact about one word.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{അവർ}} hides the person's sex, where \textbf{\ml{അവൻ}} and \textbf{\ml{അവൾ}} declare it. That makes it the safer word when you are unsure of the relationship: being a shade too polite passes without comment, and the other direction does not.

Context decides between \emph{they} and \emph{respectful he or she}, and usually decides it without effort — a room with three people in it needs no help.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ml{അവർ}
  \item the two things it can mean
  \item the pair of \emph{you}-words that work the same way
  \item which of the three third-person words hides the person's sex
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two readings of \textbf{\ml{അവർ}}? (\emph{They}, and a respectful \emph{he} or \emph{she}.) What does Malayalam use to raise the register? (A plural.) Which word would you pick if unsure? (\textbf{\ml{അവർ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ñaṅṅaḷ / nāṁ]{\ml{ഞങ്ങൾ} / \ml{നാം} — two words for \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{}, and you have to choose}

\label{lesson:ML-C71-njangal-naam}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for \emph{I}.

Now say \emph{we}. Malayalam asks you a question first, and English never has.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഞങ്ങൾ} and \ml{നാം}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞങ്ങൾ}} — \emph{ñaṅṅaḷ} — \textbf{we}, not counting the person you are talking to \textbf{\ml{നാം}} — \emph{nāṁ} — \textbf{we}, counting them in
\end{quote}

English has one \emph{we} and hides which it means. Malayalam has two and makes you pick every time.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you mean} & \textbf{you say} \\
\midrule
me and them, but not you & \ml{ഞങ്ങൾ} \\
you and me & \ml{നാം} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}We went yesterday\textquotedblright{}} said to somebody who stayed behind is \textbf{\ml{ഞങ്ങൾ}}. \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Shall we go?\textquotedblright{}} said to a friend is \textbf{\ml{നാം}} — the invitation is the whole point of it, and using \ml{ഞങ്ങൾ} there would shut them out of the sentence.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ഞങ്ങൾ}} is built on \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} — the \emph{I} you have had since chapter three — with the \textbf{-\ml{ങ്ങൾ}} plural on it. It stays inside the speaker's own group, which is the shape of the word matching the shape of the meaning.

\textbf{\ml{നാം}} is a different root and takes nobody's ending. The shorter word is the one that gathers everybody in, which is a useful thing to hold on to.

Tamil draws the same line with \emph{nāṅgaḷ} against \emph{nām}, and the two languages land on nearly the same pair of sounds — so a reader who has met one has most of the other.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ml{ഞങ്ങൾ}, \ml{നാം}
  \item which one invites a friend along
  \item which one you would use about a trip your listener missed
  \item which of the two is built on the word for \emph{I}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \emph{we} includes the listener? (\textbf{\ml{നാം}}.) Which leaves them out? (\textbf{\ml{ഞങ്ങൾ}}.) What do you ask yourself before choosing? (Whether the person listening is inside the \emph{we}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aaLukaL]{(the people) — five words, from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R71-pronoun-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the three lessons before this one. Say the word for \emph{I}, and the word for \emph{that one}, with nothing in front of you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{familiar} & \textbf{respectful} \\
\midrule
he / she & \ml{അവൻ} / \ml{അവൾ} & \ml{അവർ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{leaves you out} & \textbf{takes you in} \\
\midrule
we & \ml{ഞങ്ങൾ} & \ml{നാം} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Before this chapter a reader could say \emph{I} and \emph{you} and could not say \emph{he}, \emph{she}, \emph{they} or \emph{we}.} Seventy chapters of vocabulary with nobody in them but the two people in the room.

\begin{cousinweb}
Two of the three groups run on machinery met long ago:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{അ}-} at the front points away — the same letter that makes \textbf{\ml{അത്}} mean \emph{that one}, now doing the work on a person.
  \item \textbf{a plural raises the register} — the move that turned \textbf{\ml{നീ}} into \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}} in chapter two, turning \textbf{\ml{അവൻ}} into \textbf{\ml{അവർ}} here.
\end{itemize}

Only the two we-words are genuinely new, and the question they ask has no English equivalent to lean on.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the five words this chapter taught, from memory
  \item which one hides whether the person is a man or a woman
  \item which \emph{we} you would use to propose something to a friend
  \item the front letter three of the five share, and what it does
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word is respectful and sex-neutral? (\textbf{\ml{അവർ}}.) Which \emph{we} leaves the listener out? (\textbf{\ml{ഞങ്ങൾ}}.) What raises the register in Malayalam? (A plural.)
\end{tcolorbox}
